posts.image_prompt: A narrow carved stone tunnel deep underground in soft volcanic rock, lit by flickering oil lamps, a huge round millstone-like stone door set into the wall, chambers branching off into darkness, cinematic
posts.caption:
🕳️ A MAN KNOCKED DOWN A WALL AND FOUND A CITY

In 1963, a resident of Derinkuyu in Cappadocia, Turkey, was renovating his home. When he broke through a basement wall, he found a hidden passage.

It led to an entire underground city.

Derinkuyu goes down roughly 280 feet and has at least 18 levels. Historians estimate it could shelter up to 20,000 people, along with stables, storage and even a church.

Huge stone doors could seal it from the inside. Dozens of ventilation shafts carried fresh air deep underground.

Its origins may reach back to around the 8th century BC, and it was expanded over the centuries, at least into the Byzantine era. People still used it as a refuge into the early 20th century.

Nobody knows exactly who dug the first tunnel.

Would you have lived underground to stay safe?

👑 One pilgrimage. So much gold that its price fell.

In 1324, Mansa Musa of Mali passed through Cairo on his way to Mecca. The scholar al-Umari recorded that gold lost value there for years afterwards.

posts.image_prompt: A small square ancient steatite stamp seal carved with a bull-like animal and a few small abstract symbols above it, resting on sand at a mud-brick excavation site, warm afternoon light, macro photography
posts.caption:
🔍 A GREAT CIVILIZATION WHOSE WRITING NO ONE CAN READ

The Indus Valley Civilization built planned cities in what is now Pakistan and northwest India. Its writing flourished around 2600–1900 BC.

Archaeologists have found thousands of short inscriptions, mostly on small stone stamp seals, from dozens of sites.

The problem? They are tiny. The average inscription is only about five signs long, and none found so far is longer than about 26.

There are roughly 400 different signs, and there's no agreement on what language they record. No bilingual inscription — like Egypt's Rosetta Stone — has ever been found to help.

Do you think the Indus script will ever be deciphered?
